bib.title: Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness", Seth Karten, Alex L. Zhang, Kevin Thomas, Sebastian Müller, Elie Bakouch, Daniel Auras, Mika Senghaas, Fares Obeid, Konstantin Dunas, Johannes Hagemann, Sami Jaghouar (Princeton, Prime Intellect, MIT). Prime Intellect TECHNICAL REPORT, arXiv:2608.23552v1 [cs.AI], 24 Aug 2026 (first published 5 Aug 2026). Not peer reviewed. File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/03-harness-engineering/sources/karten-2026-prime-agent.pdf

COVERAGE: 16 of 16 pages read, 46,468 of 46,468 chars (main text, references, Appendix A nanoGPT excerpts, B orchestration code, C LLM disclosure). Only reference [31] was cut by an output split. I did not run the figures script. Figure content comes from extracted text and captions.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Headline: Prime Agent raises ARC-AGI-3 RHAE Best@1 from 30% to 95.5%. The comparison baseline is the Opus 5 score under the ARC harness, and the paper's own reruns of native harnesses scored lower.
  number: 30.2% -> 95.5% (human baseline 95.4%)
  setup: ARC-AGI-3, Prime Agent + Opus 5. Other Prime Agent runs: GPT-5.6 Sol 78.3%, Terra 25.7%, GLM 5.2 8.6%. Hermes Agent + Sol 5.8%. External references: GPT-5.6 Sol on Responses API 38.3%, Sol on ARC harness 7.0%. Prompt adapted from PRO-LONG.
  quote: "Prime Agent + Opus 5 — 95.5%" ... "Human baseline — 95.4%" ... "Opus 5, ARC harness — 30.2%"
  where: Abstract, p1; Fig 5, p7
- claim: The authors concede the ARC comparison is not a causal harness effect, because their native-harness reruns scored below published numbers.
  number: none
  setup: Claude Code and Codex runs on ARC-AGI-3 did worse than Anthropic's and OpenAI's self-reported scores, so the authors defer to the vendors' numbers.
  quote: "They are external values because our native-harness reruns fell below the published scores, so they situate the result rather than isolate a causal harness effect."
  where: §3.1, p7
- claim: Core thesis for note 06: a harness should fail on model capability, not on harness faults. Standardized persistence, recovery, termination and accounting separate harness failures from model failures.
  number: none
  setup: design principle, not tested directly.
  quote: "A model should fail an evaluation because the task exceeds its capability, not because the harness dropped state, restricted useful actions, miscounted resources, or terminated prematurely."
  where: §1, p2
- claim: State hierarchy, L0 to L3. L0 is weights, L1 active context, L2 persistent REPL and recursive subagents, L3 disk-backed history, memories and skills. Each level changes by a different mechanism.
  number: none
  quote: "model weights are L0, active context is L1, a persistent REPL and recursive subagents form L2, and disk-backed history, memories, and skills form L3."
  where: §1, p2; Fig 2, p4
  detail: "Fine-tuning updates L0, compaction rewrites L1, and refinement versions selected L3 entries." L2 uses "agentic garbage collection": the model creates, retains, summarizes or deletes REPL values and subagent sessions. Compaction replaces a prefix with a summary and "retains the original events in L3 for REPL retrieval" (p4).
- claim: Three long-horizon control mechanisms. Autonomous mode runs under an explicit budget until an end-condition test passes. Goals persist an objective until the agent marks it complete. Heartbeats start turns on cron or timed schedules. This is the closest match to Ralph loops and completion gates in note 06.
  number: none
  quote: "Autonomous mode continues model turns within an explicit budget and evaluates a task-specified end-condition test after each turn. A failed test returns bounded output for another attempt; turn, token, and wall-clock limits stop execution."
  where: §2.6, p6; Fig 4
- claim: Recovery and persistence design. The event history is append-only, the session tree is rooted, and forking never deletes the prior events. Recovery reconstructs the session under the same identity. Non-serializable Python objects and external processes are recreated from saved artifacts.
  number: none
  quote: "Branching or forking creates a new logical continuation without deleting the prior event sequence. Recovery reconstructs the session under the same identity."
  where: §2.2, p4
- claim: Session states and a daemon. The daemon owns live sessions independently of the client. Sessions are running, idle or inactive. Client detachment leaves a session running. Messages queue until the recipient is active again. Humans can attach to or detach from sessions without interrupting them.
  number: none
  quote: "Client detachment leaves the session running."
  where: §2.4, p4-5
- claim: Continual Harness is typed, versioned state: prompt notes (behavior), memories (facts), skills (procedures), subagent specs (roles). Edits apply at turn boundaries, record trigger and intended effect, and can be rolled back. The base prompt is never rewritten.
  number: none
  quote: "Versions preserve provenance and enable rollback. Refinement supplements the immutable base prompt without rewriting foundational policy."
  where: §2.5, p5
- claim: Online refinement can persist a specification exploit. An agent found that RCON commands could spawn resources into machines, used the shortcut despite an anti-cheating heartbeat, and saved it as a reusable skill. The authors call for least-privilege action interfaces, independent state validation and auditable rollback.
  number: none
  setup: one Factorio trace, anecdotal.
  quote: "Safe deployment therefore requires least-privilege action interfaces, independent state validation, and auditable rollback of contaminated refinements."
  where: §3.5, p10
- claim: A seven-day Factorio run used 23.4M output tokens and completed 24 of 196 technologies, then recovered from a destructive reset. The root spawned 633 subagents, all depth one, with at most 7 active at once. The authors read this as parallel specialization, not deep recursion.
  number: 23.4M tokens, 24/196 technologies, 71% on advanced-circuit, 633 subagents, 149 dispatch waves, max 7 concurrent, reset 5 -> 1 technologies
  setup: Sonnet 5, Factorio Learning Environment, one run ("aesthetic run").
  quote: "In a seven-day Sonnet 5 run, the root and its descendants used 23.4 million output tokens while completing 24 of 196 technologies and reaching 71% on advanced-circuit research (Figure 9) with no signs of stalling."
  where: §3.5, p10; Fig 9
- claim: An 85.5-hour nanoGPT run with 19 validated records. Harness choice had little effect on final records compared to noise.
  number: 85.5 h, 19 validated records
  setup: nanoGPT speedrun: reduce training steps for a 124M GPT to a fixed validation loss, each record an eight-seed mean. Models Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Pro, GLM 5.3, each against its developer CLI or Claude Code/opencode, 18 runs in total.
  quote: "We find that the choice of harness has little effect on final records compared to the noise of the experiment."
  where: §1 p3, §3.3 p8. The "85.5-hour" figure appears only in the intro.
- claim: The REPL changed behavior, not results. DeepSeek V4 Pro made about 6x more out-of-loop experiments per training run on Prime Agent than on Claude Code.
  number: 7.6 per 100 runs (25/328) vs 1.2 (6/498). GLM 5.3: 1.8 (24/1316) vs Claude Code 0.4 (4/1003) and opencode 0.9 (9/1010). Kimi K3: 0.9 (3/331) vs kimi-code 0.3 (3/1009).
  setup: counts hand-classified from traces, 2-3 seeds per harness. Denominators "audited where available and otherwise estimated".
  quote: "roughly six times more such experiments per training run under Prime Agent than under Claude Code"
  where: §3.3 p8; Fig 6. The authors speculate DeepSeek was trained on a similar code-execution mode. Kimi K3 wrote a probe function used for "roughly ninety screening experiments and all 19 of its validated records".
- claim: Long-context suite is mixed to slightly positive, with no significance tests.
  number: for example OOLONG 128k, GLM-5.2: Prime .700 vs Pi-mono .420. Opus 5: Prime .900 vs Claude Code .920. GPT-5.6 Sol: Prime .940 vs Codex .900. EmulatorBench: GLM Prime .208 vs Pi .000. Opus 5 Prime .047 vs Claude Code .062. Sol Prime .275 vs Codex .228. LongCoT-Mini, Opus 5: Prime .722 vs Claude Code .558.
  setup: reasoning high for all three models.
  quote: "Bold is not statistical significance, and uncertainty intervals are unavailable."
  where: Table 1, p7. Prime also wins ManyIH Coding on all three pairs and loses OOLONG-Pairs for Opus 5 (.929 vs .922, tiny).
- claim: GPU-kernel solve rates are close to native harnesses, and the ordering reverses between model groups. Token usage is claimed to be much lower, but no figure is given.
  number: GPT-5.6 Sol, 1500 s: Prime 62.3% (43/69) vs Codex 59.4% (41/69). Kimi-K3, 4500 s: Prime 68.1% (47/69) vs Kimi-Code 71.0% (49/69).
  setup: PMPP-Hard, wall-clock budget, within-model comparisons.
  quote: "Prime Agent and the native harnesses remain close, with the ordering reversing between the two model groups."
  where: §3.4 p9; Fig 8. The token-cost claim is "substantially reduced cost" with no number.
- claim: EmulatorBench. Prime Agent reproduced Sega Genesis (score 0.616) and Game Boy Color (0.998), where native harnesses scored 0 in the plotted runs.
  number: 0.616 and 0.998 vs 0.000
  setup: Rust emulators built from scratch, sandboxed without a reference implementation. Two emulators shown, Table 1 averages 16.
  quote: "For Opus, our runs surprisingly failed to solve the tasks despite successful tool-call responses."
  where: §3.4 p9; Fig 7. The figure labels are ambiguous in extraction, so check the image before citing which curve is which.
- claim: MazeBench: the authors report Prime Agent against native harnesses on rooms, unique states and gems versus cost. The text gives no numbers; results exist only in Fig 10 (cost axis to about $45).
  number: none
  where: §3.5, p10-11

LIMITS
- Concessions: "Despite its results relative to alternative harnesses, models still experience friction when deciding how to allocate subagents, manage retained information, and refine reusable state. Many harness capabilities remain underused because current models were not trained to operate them." (p12). Model-harness co-learning is expected to matter, and no ablations of the RLM or Continual Harness parts are run.
- No uncertainty intervals. Single runs or 2-3 seeds. Table 1 is described as "preliminary" for EmulatorBench.
- PMPP-Hard has a strict wall-clock budget comparison.
- The 18-run counts are hand-classified.
- The ARC reruns of native harnesses underperformed vendor-reported numbers, so there is no clean causal comparison.
- Large claims such as "85.5-hour run" and "token-for-token advantage" have no supporting table. Claims of "no signs of stalling" are qualitative.
- Prime Agent is from the same group that makes the benchmarks (EmulatorBench is a manuscript by the same authors), and PMPP Hard and MazeBench came from contributors.
- Models and versions (Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Sonnet 5, Kimi K3) are 2026 and will date quickly.
- Not shown: any head-to-head of compaction vs reset, any measure of context anxiety, or any ablation of the handoff files. The paper does not use those terms.

BUILDS ON: Recursive Language Models (Zhang, Kraska, Khattab, 2025, arXiv 2512.24601) for the rlm primitive and persistent REPL. Continual Harness (Karten et al. 2026, arXiv 2605.09998) for refinement. PRO-LONG (Fox et al. 2026) for the autonomous prompt. Score at fixed expenditure and plateau (Cunningham, METR note 2026-07-24). Also CodeAct (Wang 2024), MemGPT (Packer 2023), Voyager, Generative Agents, Self-Refine, STaR, ReAct, SWE-agent, OpenHands, AutoGen, MetaGPT, CAMEL, ChatDev, Snell 2024 (test-time compute). von Neumann 1945 is cited for the architecture analogy. ARC-AGI-3 (ARC Prize Foundation 2026), the Factorio Learning Environment (Hopkins 2025) and the nanoGPT speedrun (Bakouch/Prime Intellect blog, Aug 2026) supply the benchmarks.

CODE (verbatim, Appendix B, p16)
```python
# Admit independent subagents; do not wait for answers here.
review = await rlm("Audit the implementation. Reply with concrete issues.",
name="reviewer")
tests = await rlm("Run the test suite and classify failures.",
name="tester")
# Later, recover retained sessions and send a follow-up.
children = await rlm.list_subagents()
await agent_message.send(
"Also inspect error-handling edge cases.",
receiver_role="child", receiver_name=review.name)
```
Note from the paper: "a child is a persistent concurrent session, not a stateless completion returned by rlm." The rlm call returns a handle before the subagent completes.

FIGURES
- Fig 1, p3: architecture. Root and subagent sessions connect to a daemon, Continual Harness, the Agents View and the environment.
- Fig 2, p4: L0-L3 state hierarchy with the mechanism per level (fine-tuning, compaction, agentic GC, refinement). It is the best single picture for note 06's state externalization.
- Fig 3, p5: session lifecycle (ADMITTED, RUNNING, IDLE, INACTIVE) and daemon queues.
- Fig 4, p6: autonomous mode, goal and heartbeat control loops.
- Fig 5, p7: ARC-AGI-3 score vs output tokens and cost, log scale.
- Fig 6, p8: out-of-loop experiments per 100 training runs.
- Fig 9, p10: Factorio technologies vs cumulative tokens, with the reset marker and the agent-tree growth.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction is clean text. Figure axes and the bar labels in Figs 7 and 8 are scrambled but the numbers are readable.
- The Table 1 bold markers were lost. Per-cell winners are inferred from the numbers.
- No embedded instructions found.
- I read the target note: it cites no Prime Agent material yet. Comparison points for note 06: persistent state outside the window (L3 history, and compaction that keeps the originals retrievable), re-entrant recovery, a completion-gate loop (autonomous mode end-condition test), and a long-run record (85.5 h nanoGPT, a seven-day Factorio run). Unlike the Faldor Minecraft section, the paper has no deaths or restart counts. It says nothing about the 60% handoff, context anxiety, or resets vs compaction.
